In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an anti-reductionism that is strong enough to resist the arguments for reductionism.
the nature of emergence, the relationship between the parts of a system and the system as a whole, and how this affects our understanding of complex adaptive systems.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
reductionism is false, and that the properties of complex systems are determined by the properties of their parts, and that these properties can be derived from those of the parts.
emergent phenomena exist and are real, but they are not irreducible in any sense, and they do not have causal powers.
the laws governing a system are determined by, but not reducible to, the laws governing the parts that compose the system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in order to understand emergent phenomena, we need to know more about the properties of the lower level entities, not less.
we have developed a new approach to understanding the emergence of complex systems.
we have demonstrated a new method of creating emergent behavior in a complex, dynamic system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the traditional approach is fundamentally reductionist, but that an anti-reductionism is possible.
the reductionism vs. emergence debate is not a simple dichotomy, but rather a spectrum of possibilities that are not mutually exclusive.
there is a strong case to be made for a more radical anti-reductionism than is usually accepted.
